Garwolin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Sulbiny, Poland

Not demolished. Jewish settlement in Garwolin began toward the end of the 18th century; population reached 57% (4,141) by 1912, settling at 47.7% (2,424) by 1921, mostly deported via Parysów in November 1941 and murdered at Treblinka the following year. This cemetery was established following an October 17, 1862 perpetual lease agreement signed by Garwolin's Synagogue District representatives, who fenced the plot with a wall and embankment ditch and built a funeral house, gravedigger's apartment, and tool shed. Germans destroyed the cemetery during WWII, using hundreds of tombstones to reinforce roads, pavements, yards, and stables; the fence was destroyed and the land plowed. In 1945, the Garwolin Jewish Committee began restoration efforts, signing a July 18 contract to transport about 160 tombstones (which had been used as stable flooring) back to the cemetery; bodies exhumed from nearby towns were also relocated here, including eight people murdered at Ciechomin, reburied in 1943, and seven partisans reburied in 1948. A late-1980s Holocaust memorial project by Garwolin authorities was never completed.
